analysis.one_liner: Removes the income cap on Social Security payroll taxes so high earners pay on all wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the income cap on Social Security payroll taxes died in committee with zero cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, earnings above $117,000 (in 2014) are exempt from the Social Security payroll tax. The bill would tax earnings above that level too, raising more money for Social Security from high earners. It was introduced in December 2014, referred to the tax-writing committee, and never went anywhere before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Future and current Social Security beneficiaries benefit from stronger program financing: the tax applies to the growing share of wages that flows to people above the cap. Social Security's shortfall comes largely from the fact that a rising slice of national earnings sits above the taxable cap, so extending the tax upward closes more of the gap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $117,000, rather than stopping at the cap [S2][S3].
The same tax change applies to self-employment income, so high-earning business owners pay on income above the cap like everyone else [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people earning more than $117,000 a year pay the 12.4% combined Social Security tax on their wages above that level, roughly doubling what the highest earners currently contribute to the program. Employers of high earners also pay their half.

drawbacks.text: It is a direct tax increase on high earners, including self-employed professionals and small business owners, who would pay the full 12.4% combined rate on income above the cap [S3].

Critics of scrapping the cap generally argue it breaks the traditional link between what people pay into Social Security and the benefits they get, converting part of the program toward a redistribution-style arrangement. The bill, as summarized, raises revenue without changing benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a more solvent Social Security program paid for by the people with the most income; the cost falls entirely on households earning well above the national average. The trade-off is a straightforward values choice about whether payroll taxes should apply to all earnings. The bill itself was not a serious legislative effort: one sponsor, no cosponsors, introduced in the final weeks of a Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended three weeks later, with no cosponsors and no action.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the Scrap the Cap Act on December 11, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
The bill received no further action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the $117,000 cap keep paying Social Security tax only on their first $117,000 of earnings. Social Security's financing shortfall was not addressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoided the new tax

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to took no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: High-income households earning above the payroll tax cap
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on all earnings instead of stopping at $117,000. Their gain from the bill dying is ordinary people's loss, since Social Security's financing gap goes unfunded [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and high-earning business owners
industries.note: The bill applies the same extension to self-employment tax, so owners of pass-through businesses would pay on income above the cap too [S3].
